1Coulomb's law Roadmap
Lesson 1 · Electrostatics

Charge, Coulomb's law and superposition

About 14 minutes · two interactives · no prerequisites

QuestionWhat is the force between charges at rest?

Two charged objects at rest push or pull on each other across empty space. What exactly is that force: how does it depend on the amounts of charge, on the distance between them, and on direction? When more than two charges are present, how do the individual forces combine?

The electric field, voltage, capacitors and transistors are all built on the answer. This lesson differs from the ones that follow in one respect: nothing here is derived from a deeper law. Within classical physics these are the experimental facts from which the rest is derived. The task is to state them exactly and to understand what each part of the statement says.

Starting pointsWhat experiment establishes about charge

  • Two kinds. Matter carries a property, electric charge, that comes in two kinds. Two charges of the same kind repel; two of different kinds attract. Labelling the kinds positive and negative lets charge be a signed number q whose amounts add algebraically. Which kind is called positive is a convention; under it the electron is negative.
  • Conserved. The total charge of an isolated system, the algebraic sum of all its charges, never changes. Charge can be moved, and it can be created or destroyed only in equal and opposite amounts.
  • Quantized. Every free charge ever observed is an integer multiple of the elementary charge e = 1.602\,176\,634 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}. Since 2019 this value is exact: it is what defines the coulomb. The proton carries +e and the electron -e, equal in magnitude to at least one part in 10^{20}, which is why ordinary matter is so nearly neutral.

From mechanics we take two things: force is a vector, and forces between two bodies at rest obey Newton's third law. We also use one idealization. A point charge is a charged object whose size is negligible compared with its distance from the other charges involved.

The lawCoulomb's law

In 1785 Coulomb measured the force between small charged spheres with a torsion balance. For two point charges at rest in vacuum, q_1 at position \mathbf{r}_1 and q_2 at \mathbf{r}_2, the force on q_2 is

\mathbf{F}_{2} \;=\; \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^{2}}\,\hat{\mathbf{r}}, \qquad r = |\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1|, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{r}} = \frac{\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1}{r}

Here \hat{\mathbf{r}} is the unit vector pointing from charge 1 toward charge 2. The force on q_1 is equal and opposite, \mathbf{F}_1 = -\mathbf{F}_2. The constant \varepsilon_0, the vacuum permittivity, is measured:

\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}}, \qquad \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 8.988 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2\,C^{-2}}

Each part of the formula says something separate.

  • Direction: along the line joining the charges. Two points at rest in empty space single out exactly one direction, the line through them. A force component perpendicular to that line would have to point somewhere around it, and nothing in the situation selects where. The sign is carried by the product: if q_1 q_2 > 0 the force on q_2 is along +\hat{\mathbf{r}}, away from q_1 (repulsion); if q_1 q_2 \lt 0 it is toward q_1 (attraction). One formula covers both cases.
  • Proportional to each charge. This is tied to what "amount of charge" means. Charge is additive, and forces add (superposition, below). Two charges q placed together act as one charge 2q and exert twice the force. So the force is proportional to q_1 and, by the same argument, to q_2.
  • Inverse square of the distance. This is an experimental result, and one of the most precisely tested in physics. If the force went as 1/r^{2+\delta}, laboratory tests bound |\delta| to a few parts in 10^{16}.
  • The factor 4\pi. It is a choice of units, made so that the area of a sphere, 4\pi r^2, appears explicitly. Lesson 2 shows why that is natural: the inverse-square law is equivalent to a statement about closed surfaces surrounding the charge (Gauss's law).

For computation it is convenient to remove the unit vector. This is the form the interactives below evaluate:

\mathbf{F}_{2} \;=\; \frac{q_1 q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1}{|\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1|^{3}}
Two charges repel with force F. You halve the distance between them and also halve one of the charges. What is the new force?

Halving the distance multiplies the force by 1/(1/2)^2 = 4. Halving one charge multiplies it by 1/2. The new force is 2F. Check it on the bench: set a configuration, note F, then change r and one charge.

ScaleHow strong the electric force is

In a hydrogen atom the electron and proton are about 5.29 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m} apart. Coulomb's law gives

F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{e^2}{r^2} = \frac{(8.988\times10^{9})(1.602\times10^{-19})^2}{(5.29\times10^{-11})^2}\ \mathrm{N} \approx 8.2\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{N}

That is small in everyday terms, but it acts on an electron of mass 9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}. Compare it with the gravitational attraction between the same two particles. Both forces fall as 1/r^2, so their ratio is the same at every distance:

\frac{F_\text{electric}}{F_\text{gravity}} = \frac{e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0}{G\,m_e m_p} \approx 2.3\times10^{39}

The reason gravity dominates at large scales anyway is neutrality. Matter contains positive and negative charge in almost exactly equal amounts, so the electric forces of large bodies cancel almost completely, while mass has only one sign and always adds. The cancellation is delicate. Following an estimate in the Feynman Lectures: if two people at arm's length each had one percent more electrons than protons, each would carry roughly 3\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{C} of excess charge, and the repulsion between them would be of order 10^{25}\ \mathrm{N}, comparable to the weight of a mass equal to the Earth's at the Earth's surface (6\times10^{25}\ \mathrm{N}).

Second lawSuperposition

Coulomb's law speaks only about two charges. For more than two, experiment adds a separate fact, the principle of superposition: the force on a charge due to several others is the vector sum of the forces that each would exert if it were alone. The presence of a third charge does not alter the force between the first two.

For a charge q_0 at \mathbf{r}_0 and source charges q_1, \dots, q_N at \mathbf{r}_1, \dots, \mathbf{r}_N:

\mathbf{F}_0 \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{q_0\, q_i}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{\mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r}_i}{|\mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r}_i|^{3}}

Three things follow at once.

  • Superposition is not a consequence of Coulomb's law. A world in which pairs obey Coulomb's law but a third charge modifies the pair force is logically possible. Experiment says ours is not like that.
  • The sum is over vectors. Magnitudes do not add; components do.
  • q_0 multiplies every term, so it factors out of the sum. What remains depends only on the source charges and on the point \mathbf{r}_0. That remaining vector is the electric field, the subject of Lesson 2.
A charge of +4 nC and a charge of +1 nC are fixed 9 cm apart. Is there a point where a third charge feels no net force? Roughly where, and does it matter what the third charge is?

Use the "+4 and +1" preset on the bench and drag the test charge until the readout reports zero net force. Then switch the test charge to −1 nC or +2 nC and see whether the point moves. The worked answer is in "Check yourself", question 1.

ResultWhat is now established

Coulomb's law. Two point charges at rest in vacuum exert on each other a force along the line joining them, proportional to the product of the charges and to the inverse square of their separation, repulsive for like signs and attractive for unlike signs.

Superposition. With several charges present, the force on any one is the vector sum of the Coulomb forces from each of the others.

Limits of validity. Charges at rest: moving charges also exert magnetic forces, and changes propagate at finite speed (Lessons 9 to 12). Point charges, or bodies small compared with their separation: for extended bodies, apply the law to each element of charge and sum. Vacuum: inside matter the surrounding charges respond and must be included (Lesson 8). Superposition is exact in classical electrodynamics; quantum electrodynamics predicts departures only at field strengths of order 10^{18}\ \mathrm{V/m}, far beyond anything in a circuit.

ConnectionsWhere this leads

  • Electronics Foundations 2: The electric field and Gauss's law (not built yet). Dividing out the test charge turns the force law into a field defined at every point.
  • Astrophysics 1: Newtonian gravity: the other inverse-square law (not built yet). Newton's law of gravitation has the same inverse-square form, so every mathematical result of the next lessons (field, Gauss's law, potential) carries over to gravity with mass in place of charge and one sign instead of two.
  • Chip Making 2: Doping, carriers and the p-n junction (not built yet). The Coulomb attraction between an electron and an ionized dopant atom, weakened by the surrounding silicon, sets how easily dopants give up their carriers.

Check yourselfThree questions

Charges of +4 nC at x = 0 and +1 nC at x = 9 cm are fixed. Where on the line between them is the net force on a third charge zero? Does the answer depend on the third charge? Is the third charge in stable equilibrium there?

Between the charges the two forces on the third charge are opposite in direction. They cancel where the magnitudes are equal:

\frac{4}{x^2} = \frac{1}{(9\ \mathrm{cm} - x)^2} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{x}{9\ \mathrm{cm} - x} = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; x = 6\ \mathrm{cm}

The third charge q_0 multiplies both terms and cancels, so the point is the same for any q_0 of either sign. On Bench 2 this point is 1.5 cm to the right of centre.

Stability: a positive q_0 displaced along the line is pushed back, but displaced sideways it is pushed further out. A negative q_0 behaves the opposite way. In neither case is the equilibrium stable in all directions. Lesson 2 shows this is general: no arrangement of fixed charges can hold another charge in stable equilibrium in empty space.

Two identical small metal spheres carry +6 nC and −2 nC and attract each other with force F at separation r. They are touched together and returned to the same separation r, which is large compared with their size. What is the force now?

Charge is conserved: the total is +4\ \mathrm{nC}. The spheres are identical, so by symmetry each ends with +2\ \mathrm{nC}. Before, the product of the charges was -12\ \mathrm{nC^2}; after, it is +4\ \mathrm{nC^2}. The force is now repulsive with magnitude F/3.

On Bench 2 with two equal positive charges, the test charge sits on the perpendicular bisector. Each source alone exerts a force of magnitude F₁ on it. Why is the net force less than 2F₁, and in which direction does it point?

Forces add as vectors. By the mirror symmetry of the arrangement, the components along the line joining the sources are equal and opposite and cancel; the components along the bisector are equal and add. If each force makes angle \theta with the bisector, the net force is 2F_1\cos\theta, directed along the bisector away from the sources. It equals 2F_1 only in the limit of large distance, where \theta \to 0 and the pair acts as a single charge of twice the size.

Build sparkMeasure the inverse-square law yourself

A balance that resolves 0.001 g resolves a force of about 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{N}, which is the size of the forces on Bench 1. Rest a small metallised sphere on an insulating post on the balance pan, hold an identical one on an insulating rod directly above it, charge both by touching them with the same charged object, and record the change in reading against the gap. Plot force against distance on log-log axes and measure the slope. The departures from −2 are instructive: at small gaps the spheres are not point charges, and charge leaks away over minutes in humid air.
